extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, constitutional design, and history
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply principles for designing and judging constitutions and state institutions (checks and balances, role of laws, executive design, elections, education, property, factions) in republican and monarchical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and balances necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Checks and balances necessary (I. iv.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance of power is a required structural principle in republics; the text repeatedly emphasizes creating opposing powers to prevent tyranny and preserve liberty (see related notes on a triple balance of powers and three branches of power existing in every society).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of power aimed at in republics
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance of power, aimed at in all republics (I. 93; I. ix.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Republican constitutions should intentionally distribute authority (landed property, army, senate, popular bodies) so no single interest predominates; this is presented as a central design goal of good governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government of laws vs government of men
rubrics_metrics.description: Nation cannot be free except governed by fixed laws; distinction between a government of laws and of men (I. 124–126).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions should prioritize rule by stable, fixed laws rather than discretionary rule by particular rulers; laws are the safeguard of freedom and must be clearly distinguished from arbitrary personal power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative executive power required
rubrics_metrics.description: No constitution can be defended without a negative executive power (III. 294).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A separate executive with a negative (veto/override) function is necessary to prevent legislative excesses and to secure liberties; design should include mechanisms for executive check on other branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive power concentrated but bound by law
rubrics_metrics.description: True policy to place the executive power in one man; No man to exalt himself above the law (III. 460–461).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrating executive authority in a single person can be effective for administering justice and representing the state's majesty, but that executive must be legally constrained so personal aggrandizement is prevented.

rubrics_metrics.name: People as an essential legislative branch (but not sole)
rubrics_metrics.description: People an essential branch of the legislature, as being most sensible of their own burdens (III. 295); the people should have a share in government but not necessarily be the sole assembly (III. 326).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs should include popular representation because the people are primarily affected by laws, but their power should be tempered through coequal institutions (senate/executive) to prevent majoritarian oppression or instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed government is preferable
rubrics_metrics.description: A mixed one (mixed government) most proper to do justice to all men; a triple balance of equal powers an effectual remedy against factions (III. 447; III. 433).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine elements of monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy so different interests check one another; explicit multi-headed legislatures/executives can reduce factional harms and restrain luxury and corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentrating power in a single assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: Government not to be trusted in a single assembly; disadvantages from appointments being made by a single assembly (I. 133; I. 372).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrating appointment and legislative power in one body creates risks (committees, abuses, faction); institutional design should distribute appointment and oversight functions across bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and discipline must be supported for free government
rubrics_metrics.description: Education and discipline lose their force when unsupported by law; more indispensable and general under a free government than any other; must be supported by private munificence (III. 476).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public virtue and stability depend on broad education and civic discipline; constitutional design should encourage and enable education (including private support) to underpin liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elections as schools of political art; integrity required
rubrics_metrics.description: Elections, the best schools of political art and address (III. 274); various illegal methods at elections described (III. 274 et seq.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elections should be structured to educate citizens and produce capable officeholders; protect electoral integrity by prohibiting illegal methods and designing transparent procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws should guard against what men may do
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws are intended to guard against what men may do (I. 132).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law's purpose is preventative and protective; legal frameworks should anticipate human misconduct and constrain it via clear rules rather than rely on rulers' virtue alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property security is essential to liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Essential to liberty that their property should be secure; the rich have as much right to their liberty and property as the poor (III. 328).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design must ensure property rights protection for all social classes as a foundation for equal liberty and social stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factions produce ill consequences; structural remedies required
rubrics_metrics.description: Factions and divisions have ill consequences (III. 131; III. 432); a triple balance of equal powers an effectual remedy against them (III. 433).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional separation and balance are the primary remedies for factionalism; design should reduce incentives and capacities for partisan violence or dominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws' authority depends on vigilance and constancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws owe their perpetual seniority to vigilance and constancy; laws alone to be trusted with unlimited confidence (III. 453; III. 281–282).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain and defend the rule of law through continuous institutional vigilance, not by assuming laws once written will be self-sustaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit successive representatives to avoid corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Successive representatives use power for the express purposes of corruption (III. 342).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term limits, rotation in office, and other anti-entrenchment mechanisms should be used to prevent consolidation of power and corruption among serial officeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear and deterrence have a role in governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear, necessity of, in every kind of government (III. 487).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should include credible deterrents (laws, penalties, oversight) to restrain misconduct and preserve order, balanced against the need to protect liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers from committees and concentrated executive appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: Dangers to be apprehended from committees; danger from electing a governor or president (I. 376; I. 376–376).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully define and constrain committees' remit and appointment powers; avoid leaving pivotal appointments to narrow, temporary committees without checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: People's rights more secure when tempered by separate executive and aristocratic senate
rubrics_metrics.description: People, their rights more secure when their power is tempered by a separate executive, and an aristocratical senate (III. 348).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design should combine popular participation with independent institutions (executive, senate/upper chamber) that moderate popular impulses and safeguard long-term interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent democratic devices can be hazardous if misapplied
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons selected from among the people a hazardous experiment, tried by the Americans with doubtful success (III. 296).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious implementing purely popular selection mechanisms for high office without safeguards; experimental democratic methods require institutional supports to work safely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed government restrains luxury and corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: A triple balance in the legislature is the only remedy against luxury; mixed government restrains luxury and tends to check tyranny (III. 337–339).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional blending—monarchical/aristocratic/democratic elements—reduces the material and moral drivers of corruption and excessive luxury among elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive represents the majesty of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive power represents the majesty of the people (III. 419).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The executive should embody and protect the public interest; design must give it authority to act effectively while remaining accountable to law and other institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws may oppress minorities if made by simple majority
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws made by a majority may oppress a minority (I. 123).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include constitutional or institutional protections (checks, upper chambers, vetoes, judicial review) to prevent majoritarian tyranny against minority rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: No constitution should rely on perpetual vigilance of virtue alone
rubrics_metrics.description: All projects formed upon a supposition of continual vigilance and virtue cheat and delude (III. 412).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional design should not presume continuous civic virtue; instead, embed structural constraints and incentives that operate even when virtue is imperfect.
